site.name: atlas-tutor
site.summary: atlas-tutor Fictional AI math & CS tutor "Atlas Tutor" chat fixture. UXBench fixture in the Chatbot / Agent Interface category. Layout **Three-column desktop:** - **Left rail (260 px)** — branded sidebar with New-chat button, search, Subjects nav (Mathematics / Programming / Physics / Statistics / Linear algebra with counts), and threaded history grouped by recency (Today / Last 7 days / Earlier — 11 threads total). Sticky profile-mini footer with streak badge. - **Center (flex)** — conversation viewport with sticky head ("Chain rule — when both functions move" · model · last reply · 3 head-tools); messages area centered to 820 px; sticky composer at the bottom with attach / textarea (Cmd+Enter to send) / mic / send-button row plus suggestion chips and a model selector. - **Right rail (320 px)** — practice problems panel (6 chain-rule problems with difficulty pills / hint button / 3-state Solve→Submit→Correct toggle), Concepts card (4 internal links), Your progress card with progress bar updated as practice is completed. Conversation pre-fill

run_plan.goal: Exhaustively explore and critique the UX of the atlas-tutor system, focusing on the primary settings/privacy flow, chat interactions, practice panel, and responsive mobile layout.
run_plan.summary: The exploration will proceed by first validating the primary settings/privacy flow via the profile footer. Next, it will exercise the core chat interface including composer controls, message actions, and thread navigation. The right-rail practice and concepts panel will be tested for state changes and interactions. Finally, all critical paths will be re-validated on a mobile viewport to assess responsive behavior and layout warnings.
assumptions: The ⚙ button in the bottom left profile footer is the primary entry point for the settings/privacy flow.
The practice problems in the right rail are interactive and can change state (e.g., Solve → Submit → Correct).
The chat interface supports simulated interactions like sending messages, copying, and sharing.
The site is a single-page application with index.html serving as the sole view.
risk_hotspots: Settings/Privacy modal or view triggered by the small ⚙ button (22x21px, high risk for mobile tap failures)
Right rail practice problem state toggles (Solve→Submit→Correct) potentially failing to update the progress bar
Message action buttons (👍, 👎, Copy, Share) which have small tap targets (32x29px) and may cause mis-taps on mobile
Chat composer attachment (📎) and microphone (🎤) buttons which may lack clear feedback or functionality

phases.title: Settings & Privacy Flow
phases.objective: Locate, open, and interact with the settings/privacy controls, validating the primary user goal.
key_checks: Click the ⚙ button in the profile footer to open settings/privacy
Verify presence of privacy controls and account settings
Toggle privacy settings and confirm state retention
Close settings and verify return to main chat view
exit_criteria: Settings/privacy view has been fully interacted with
All visible toggles/inputs in the settings have been exercised

phases.title: Core Chat Interactions
phases.objective: Validate the central chat experience including composing, sending, and interacting with messages.
key_checks: Type in the textarea and send a message using the → button
Click suggestion chips (e.g., 'tan(√x) — derive it') to populate/send
Interact with message actions: 👍, 👎, 📋 Copy, ⤴ Share, ↻ Try again
Use the search input in the left rail to filter threads
Click a historical thread from 'LAST 7 DAYS' or 'EARLIER' to load it

phases.title: Practice Panel & Right Rail
phases.objective: Exercise the practice problems, hints, and concepts links in the right rail.
key_checks: Click '▶ Practice' in the header to ensure right rail focus
Click the hint button on a practice problem
Cycle a practice problem through its states: Solve → Submit → Correct
Verify the 'Your progress' bar updates after solving a problem
Click a concept link (e.g., 'Chain rule') and observe the outcome
exit_criteria: At least one practice problem fully solved

phases.title: Left Rail Navigation & New Chat
phases.objective: Test sidebar navigation, subject filters, and new chat creation.
key_checks: Click '+ New chat' button and verify the view resets
Click a subject filter (e.g., 'Programming 7') and verify thread list updates
Click the 'Atlas Tutor' logo link at the top

phases.title: Mobile Viewport Validation
phases.objective: Re-test critical flows and check layout warnings on a mobile viewport.
key_checks: Switch to mobile viewport and verify layout adaptation (e.g., collapsible rails)
Re-open settings/privacy via the ⚙ button on mobile
Attempt to send a chat message on mobile
Validate tap targets for 👍/👎 and action buttons on small screen
Check if right rail (Practice/Concepts) is accessible on mobile
exit_criteria: Mobile layout rendered without major overflow
Primary settings and chat flows functional on mobile
Small tap target warnings reviewed in context

coverage_targets.features: Interact with all 40 buttons, 5 links, 2 inputs, and validate right-rail state changes
coverage_targets.mobile: Repeat settings, chat, and practice flows on mobile viewport; verify handling of small tap targets

notes: Pay special attention to the ⚙ button's small size (22x21px) during mobile testing as flagged by layout warnings.
The practice problem state toggle (Solve→Submit→Correct) is a complex custom control that needs careful step-by-step validation.
Since there is only one HTML file, deep state exploration (modals, views) within the page is critical.

observation.title: Atlas Tutor — math & CS tutor
observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? LAST 7 DAYS Eigenvalues of a 3 × 3 matrix Bayes' theorem — disease testing Binary search — off-by-one bugs Why does e^x derive to itself? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Explain Markov chains ⌘↵ to send · model · Atlas-3 ↓ PRACTICE PROBLEMS Chain rule Difficulty · level 2 1 EASY d/dx sin(3x + 2) Solve 💡 Hint 2 EASY d/dx (x² + 1)5 Solve 💡 Hint 3 MEDIUM d/dx e^(cos(x)) Solve 💡 Hint 4 MEDIUM d/dx tan(√x) Solve 💡 Hint 5 HARD d/dx ln(sin(x³)) Solve 💡 Hint 6 HARD d/dx (sec(2x))3 Solve 💡 Hint Concepts in this thread Chain rule Calculus · 5 min Derivatives of trig functions Calculus · 3 min Composing functions Pre-calc · 4 min Notation: f', dy/dx, ḟ Calculus · 2 min Your progress Today 4 / 10 problems Streak 14 days · 🔥 Topic mastery Chain rule · 72%

Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? LAST 7 DAYS Eigenvalues of a 3 × 3 matrix Bayes' theorem — disease testing Binary search — off-by-one bugs Why does e^x derive to itself? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? LAST 7 DAYS Eigenvalues of a 3 × 3 matrix Bayes' theorem — disease testing Binary search — off-by-one bugs Why does e^x derive to itself? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA How do I differentiate cos(x³)? A Got it — I'd start by identifying the layers. For something like How do I differentiate cos(x³)?, write out the outer and inner functions, derive each, and stack with the chain rule. Open practice problem #4 on the right and try this same recipe. 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA How do I differentiate cos(x³)? A Got it — I'd start by identifying the layers. For something like How do I differentiate cos(x³)?, write out the outer and inner functions, derive each, and stack with the chain rule. Open practice problem #4 on the right and try this same recipe. 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? LAST 7 DAYS Eigenvalues of a 3 × 3 matrix Bayes' theorem — disease testing Binary search — off-by-one bugs Why does e^x derive to itself? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA How do I differentiate cos(x³)? A Got it — I'd start by identifying the layers. For something like How do I differentiate cos(x³)?, write out the outer and inner functions, derive each, and stack with the chain rule. Open practice problem #4 on the right and try this same recipe. 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? LAST 7 DAYS Eigenvalues of a 3 × 3 matrix Bayes' theorem — disease testing Binary search — off-by-one bugs Why does e^x derive to itself? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA How do I differentiate cos(x³)? A Got it — I'd start by identifying the layers. For something like How do I differentiate cos(x³)?, write out the outer and inner functions, derive each, and stack with the chain rule. Open practice problem #4 on the right and try this same recipe. 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Explain Markov chains ⌘↵ to send · model · Atlas-3 ↓ PRACTICE PROBLEMS Chain rule Difficulty · level 2 1 EASY d/dx sin(3x + 2) Submit 💡 Hint Hint · identify the outer and inner functions in sin(3x + 2). observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? LAST 7 DAYS Eigenvalues of a 3 × 3 matrix Bayes' theorem — disease testing Binary search — off-by-one bugs Why does e^x derive to itself? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA How do I differentiate cos(x³)? A Got it — I'd start by identifying the layers. For something like How do I differentiate cos(x³)?, write out the outer and inner functions, derive each, and stack with the chain rule. Open practice problem #4 on the right and try this same recipe. 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Explain Markov chains ⌘↵ to send · model · Atlas-3 ↓ PRACTICE PROBLEMS Chain rule Difficulty · level 2 1 EASY d/dx sin(3x + 2) Submit 💡 Hint Hint · identify the outer and inner functions in sin(3x + 2). observation.title: Atlas Tutor — math & CS tutor
observation.visible_text: Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 ✓ ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? observation.title: Atlas Tutor — math & CS tutor
observation.visible_text: Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? observation.visible_text: Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA How do I solve quadratic equations? A Thinking… 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Explain Markov chains ⌘↵ to send · model · Atlas-3 ↓
